problems.stem: Three teams pitch a software case for their design project. Which selection rationale is strongest for a graduate ID case study?
options: We chose the tool with the most features so we have room to grow.
We chose this tool because its core affordance, branching scenarios, directly supports our learning goal of decision practice, and our learner and time constraints fit its setup cost.
We chose the newest tool because it is trending.
We chose the tool our instructor seemed to like.
problems.explanation: A defensible case selection ties a specific affordance of the tool to the learning goal and checks fit against learner and resource constraints, rather than counting features.

problems.stem: A team starts by listing the flashy features of a VR tool, then tries to invent a learning goal that uses them. Why does this sequence weaken the case?
options: Because VR is never appropriate for instruction.
Because it reverses the design logic: the learning goal and audience should drive tool selection, not the tool's features driving the goal.
Because flashy features always improve learning outcomes.
Because teams should choose tools without considering features at all.
problems.explanation: Goal-first design selects a tool whose affordances serve a defined goal. Feature-first selection produces solutions in search of a problem.

problems.stem: Two tools can both reach the learning goal. Tool A needs a 2-week build and paid licenses; Tool B needs 3 days and is free for the cohort. The case study still picks Tool A with no stated reason. What is the selection flaw?
options: There is no flaw; the more expensive tool is always more rigorous.
The case ignores constraint analysis: when goal fit is comparable, cost, time, and access constraints should justify the choice, and an unexamined pick is not defensible.
Free tools can never meet a learning goal.
The team should pick whichever tool has more buttons.
problems.explanation: When affordance fit is comparable, the defensible case weighs constraints such as time, cost, and learner access. A choice made without that analysis is not justified.

problems.stem: What single piece of evidence best demonstrates that a chosen software case actually fits the instructional problem?
options: A screenshot showing the tool looks modern.
A short mapping that links each learning objective to the specific tool affordance that supports it, with constraints noted.
A list of every feature the tool offers.
A note that the team enjoyed using the tool.
problems.explanation: An objective-to-affordance mapping with constraints makes the fit inspectable, showing the case was selected for the problem rather than for novelty.
